title: Intervals
summary: Sort intervals by start time, then sweep left to right merging or comparing each one against the last one you kept.
explanation: Interval problems (merging overlapping ranges, inserting a new interval, finding free time, counting overlaps) almost always start the same way: sort the intervals by start time. Once sorted, you never need to compare an interval against anything except the most recently processed one, which turns an apparently O(n^2) pairwise comparison problem into an O(n log n) single sweep.

For merging, walk the sorted intervals and keep a 'current merged interval'. If the next interval's start is less than or equal to the current merged interval's end, they overlap — extend the current interval's end to the max of the two ends. If it starts after the current interval ends, there's a gap: push the current interval to the result and start a new current interval from this one.

The same sort-then-sweep idea generalizes: for 'can you attend all meetings' you just check no two sorted intervals overlap; for 'minimum meeting rooms' you track how many intervals are simultaneously open using a small heap or a sweep over start/end events; for 'insert interval' you merge the new interval into its sorted position in one pass instead of resorting from scratch.
whenToUse: The input is a list of (start, end) ranges and you need to merge, insert, or detect overlaps between them.
You need to know the maximum number of overlapping intervals at once (e.g. minimum meeting rooms).
A brute-force pairwise comparison of all intervals would be O(n^2), but sorting by start time collapses it to one sweep.
The problem talks about scheduling, calendars, or ranges that can overlap and need to be consolidated.
timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the sweep
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the output (or O(log n) to O(n) for the sort, depending on implementation)
